pages.text: Some sums are too hard to work out. Throw dice instead: average N random samples and the answer is off by only $(thing)σ/√N$(). To halve the error, sample four times as much. The $(item)Monte Carlo Engine$() draws up to a trillion samples a run.
$(thing)Importance sampling$() draws more samples where they matter. Set near the problem's own optimum it cuts σ several times; set wrong, it makes σ worse than plain sampling.

Every sample erases bits, and $(thing)Landauer's principle$() says erasing a bit gives off at least kT·ln 2: the engine's heat is proportional to its own temperature. Cool the cores and a trillion samples cost far less.

Sums of random numbers fall on a bell curve - the central limit theorem - so the engine grows Normal Distribution Crystals; and its Markov chains sample a posterior without ever computing it, turning two Prior Tablets into four Posteriors.
